title: Watchfulness
hookLine: the first rung: simply paying attention to how you live
last: THE PATH OF THE JUST BEGINS WITH THE OBVIOUS.

cards: Some evenings the drive home simply disappears. Keys in the door, coat on the hook, and no memory of a single traffic light. The body made every turn.

Nobody was watching. Plenty of days go that way too: answered, eaten, scrolled, slept, with the person living them somewhere else. Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto put a remedy for that on the very bottom rung of his ladder.
Before zeal, before purity, before holiness, the first trait he asks for is the one that makes the others possible.

teach.h: LOOK AT YOUR OWN DEEDS AND WAYS.
teach.b: Zehirut. Watchfulness. Turn it four ways.
First, what it is. In Mesillat Yesharim, watchfulness means a person looks carefully at their own deeds and ways: is this good, is this not, where is it heading? Not a mood.
A habit of checking. Second, life without it.

teach.h: A BLIND MAN ON A RIVERBANK.
teach.b: Someone who goes through life without watching, Luzzatto says, is like a blind man walking along the bank of a river. The danger is real and close, and he doesn't see it.
Nothing has gone wrong yet, and that's what makes the riverbank frightening. Third, why people skip it. Luzzatto doesn't blame laziness first.
He blames the rush: daily life presses so hard that people never get a quiet moment to look where they're going.

He reaches for a line from Jeremiah about a horse charging headlong into battle, too fast to see what's in front of it. A good-hearted person can still be that horse. Fourth, the Tanakh's short version.
The prophet Haggai, speaking to people busy with their own houses while the Temple lay unbuilt, says it twice: "Consider your ways."

Some Mussar teachers pair this with heshbon hanefesh, an accounting of the soul at day's end, but zehirut starts earlier: mid-day, mid-drive, catching yourself while it's happening. It isn't suspicion of yourself.
It's being present for your own life, so the rest of the ladder has someone standing on it.

how: Mussar students begin Mesillat Yesharim with zehirut, watchfulness, often practicing it by pausing during the day to notice their own actions, alongside a nightly accounting of the soul.

o: fear of danger in the world outside
careful attention to how you're living

p: a blind man on a riverbank

s: Luzzatto blames the lack of watchfulness mainly on laziness
he points first to the rush: daily busyness leaves no quiet moment to look.
watchfulness is the first rung of the ladder
in Mesillat Yesharim it comes before zeal, purity and holiness.
zehirut means being suspicious of yourself
it means looking at your own deeds and ways: being present for your own life.

games.q: you're Luzzatto, explaining why good people fail to watch their lives. what do you point to first?
o: the rush of daily life leaves no time to look.
games.why: he describes people pressed by busyness, like a horse rushing headlong into battle, with no quiet moment to look.

practice: Choose one hour later today, the commute, an afternoon at your desk, the evening at home, and one thing to watch for in it: how you speak when tired, what your hands reach for when bored, whether you're really listening.
Rehearse the moment of noticing, a small inner glance, a quiet there I am, with no judging and no fixing. Then simply notice yourself breathing right now, and if you pray, you can ask for open eyes.

wordCard.voice: Zehirut. Watchfulness: paying careful attention to how you live. The first rung of Luzzatto's ladder in Mesillat Yesharim. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: watchfulness, care; the first trait in Mesillat Yesharim.

carryVoice: Your line: be watchful. Seeing yourself comes before fixing anything. Eyes open; see you soon.
